title: The Chafetz Chaim (Psalm 34:13–14)
hook: Israel Meir Kagan's book on speech takes its name from "Who is the man that desireth life"

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lashon hara, and your line was no gossip. Did a name come up, and did you find your sentence? Today, the book that gathered the rules for it. Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

A peddler is walking through the towns of Galilee, calling out like any street seller: who wants to buy the elixir of life? A rabbi named Yannai, studying nearby, hears him and calls him over. The peddler doesn't open a bottle. He opens a book of Psalms and points to a verse. That's the story the midrash tells. The verse he pointed to would one day give its name to a book, and the book would give its name to the man who wrote it. Today's word is that name.
screen: `WHO WANTS THE ELIXIR OF LIFE?` → `HE OPENS THE PSALMS.` → `A VERSE BECOMES A NAME.`

segments.voice: The Chafetz Chaim. In Hebrew, chafetz chaim means desiring life. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Psalm thirty-four, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, asks: "Who is the man that desireth life, and loveth days, that he may see good therein?" It's a question with a lot of hands going up. Then comes the answer: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." Not a diet. Not a medicine. The tongue. Second, the book. A rabbi named Israel Meir Kagan, living among the Jews of Eastern Europe, wrote a book gathering the laws of guarding speech: what counts as lashon hara, when speaking is forbidden, when it's required to protect someone. He named the book from this verse: Chafetz Chaim. Third, the man who became his book. People came to call the author by the book's title, and the name stuck: the Chafetz Chaim. It's an unusual kind of fame, being named for a book about what not to say. Fourth, the next verse. The psalm doesn't stop at keeping quiet. It goes on: depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it. Guarding the tongue isn't only a fence. It's a way of making room for peace. Yesterday named the harm. Today hands it a discipline, with a verse at the front of it. And the question still stands open: who wants life?
screen: `WHO IS THE MAN THAT DESIRETH LIFE?` · `A BOOK OF THE LAWS OF SPEECH.` · `THE MAN BECAME HIS BOOK.` · `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.` · then, large: `KEEP THY TONGUE FROM EVIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your tongue today. Settle, and breathe. Touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your teeth. Feel how small it is, and how much it does. Now run through your day ahead. Who will you talk with? Where will the conversation be easy to tilt? Pick one moment and decide in advance what you'll do if a story starts: let it pass, or turn it toward something good. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line, keep thy tongue from evil, as a reminder. If you don't, simply hold the question: who wants life? The bell holds the time.
The Chafetz Chaim. Desiring life: the psalm's question, the title of Israel Meir Kagan's book on guarding speech, and the name people gave the man. Today's word.
Your line: keep thy tongue from evil. Today, when you feel a story about someone forming in your mouth, pause one breath, and ask whether it seeks peace. Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Some Jews study a short section of the Chafetz Chaim's laws of speech each day, often in study groups or with a daily calendar, and Psalm 34's verses on the tongue are sung in some prayer services.
